name: Northern Tepehuan
confidence_why: Gil Burgoin's first-hand acoustic description of the Baborigame dialect (2021, JIPA Illustration and AMP 9 paper) establishes Northern Tepehuan as a tone language with a single culminative high tone and predictable, non-contrastive stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the first or second syllable of longer words, and the only dissent is Bascom's one- remark that stress 'fluctuates freely in many words', an older impressionistic note that Gil Burgoin 2021 reports is not borne out by the word lists in Bascom & Molina 1998.

catalog_quote: [JIPA 2021, 'Tone and word stress'] Northern Tepehuan is a tonal language with a single phonological tone: the high tone H. ... the H tone is culminative, i.e., it occurs at most once in a phonological word ... Stress is predictable from the size and the tonal pattern of the word. Stress falls on the first syllable in disyllabic words – regardless of lexical tone or vowel duration as shown in (4) and (5) above – and on the second syllable in phonologically toneless words with three or more syllables, as in /ipuːrai/ [iˈpuːrɛi] ‘dress’ or /nakasɨrai/ [naˈqasɨrɛi] ‘scorpion’. However, when a H tone is phonologically specified in the first syllable and the word has three or more syllables, the stress always falls in the H syllable, as in /úːridɨ/ [ˈúːʎiɟɨ] ‘his maternal grandmother’, in contrast, for instance, with /iːbɨxi/ [iːˈbɨxi] ‘he/she breathes’, and /taːtasai/ [taːˈtasəi] ‘he/she splits’. [AMP 9 2021, sec. 5.1, pp. 3-4] NTep stress is generally predictable from the number of syllables of the word and from syllable weight, although there are a number of relevant exceptions. ... The first stage observes disyllabic words, which, as stated above, are always stress-initial. ... (4) Stress is never final ... (5) i. stress falls on the first heavy 𝞂 ii. otherwise it falls on the second 𝞂
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Northern Tepehuan is not in the catalog. The one works with stress in the title (Glottolog 669887, author-less) is Kim, Michael Jinhwa 1997, WCCFL 15: 257-272, a metrical reanalysis of Bascom's data claiming tone is predictable from stress; this search of works with stress in the title instead turned up and read two open first-hand sources by Carlos Gil Burgoin: AMP 9 (2021), which gives an explicit rule (stress never final; disyllables initial; longer words: first heavy syllable, else second syllable; L-toned initial long vowels repel stress; NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT) with acoustic backing, and the CLECM 7 (2020) critical bibliography, which documents that Bascom 1982: 272 called stress non-contrastive and freely fluctuating, that Woo 1970 does not treat stress, and that Kim 1997 works from Bascom's data. Bascom 1982 (SIL sketch, now could not be reached by automated download/print), Bascom 1959 and Woo 1970 (paywalled DOIs) remain unread; Bascom 1982 is the high-priority acquisition. Recommended new record: weight-sensitive initial-window stress, deciding source Gil Burgoin 2021 sec. 5.

new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per word, never on the final syllable. Disyllables are always stressed on the first syllable regardless of weight or pitch. In words of three or more syllables, stress falls on the first heavy syllable (long vowel, consonant coda or glide coda), otherwise on the second syllable ([ˈúːrugi] 'bird', [ˈtáʃkaʎi] 'tortilla' vs. [baˈtópa] 'fish'). Suffixation of a light-light disyllable moves stress to the second syllable ([ˈúsù] > [ùˈsúdɨ̀]). Modelled as NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned. The author assumes Hyman's culminativity (at most one stress per word, sec. 3) and describes a single prominence 'always in the first or second syllable' (p. 1).
new_statements.exceptions: (1) Suffixed forms of disyllables with the L.H pitch pattern (lexical L on the long first vowel) stress the second syllable although the first is heavy: [ˈbàːbá] + dɨ > [bàːˈbádɨ̀] 'grandfather.3s' (sec. 5.2). (2) Some morphologically simple polysyllables have an unstressed initial long vowel: [iːˈbɨ́hɨj] 'breath', [taːˈtámwi] 'tooth' (sec. 5.3). Both are attributed to a lexical low tone repelling stress (*ALIGN(HEAD/LOW), sec. 6). Note that Bascom 1982: 272 had instead claimed 'Stress is noncontrastive. It is freely fluctuation [sic] in many words.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in a tonal language (analysed as privative /L/; earlier work as H vs. L). Evidence: a 1200-entry lexical base, F0 measurements on 692 disyllabic tokens, two female speakers from Tupuri village, Baborigame, Chihuahua. Stress cued by an intonational H* on the stressed syllable except in L-toned words, where the pitch peak is on the following syllable. Bascom 1982 (grammar sketch, p. 272) and Bascom 2003 (draft grammar, sec. 0.1) give no placement rule; Gil Burgoin's 2021 JIPA Illustration (paywalled) is reported by its abstract to refine the rule (stress on the first syllable of disyllables, typically the second syllable of longer toneless words, aligned with a first-syllable H in 3+ syllable words).
new_statements.identity_note: Gil Burgoin's data come from two female speakers of the Tupuri village, Baborigame, Chihuahua, i.e. the Baborigame dialect, which Bascom 1982: 271 calls the larger of the two major dialects (the other is Nabogame). Bascom 1982/2003 and Bascom & Molina 1998 are also Baborigame. No separate Glottolog dialect code is known to me; the language-level code nort2959 applies.

The JIPA Illustration gives the same placement facts (sigma-1 in disyllables, sigma-1 or sigma-2 in longer words, never outside the first two syllables) and so agrees on placement, but it conditions the sigma-1/sigma-2 choice on lexical H tone rather than syllable weight and says nothing about weight; words with a long first vowel and no H (/iːbɨxi/, /taːtasai/) take sigma-2 st…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tonal language with one privative tone (H, culminative, confined to the first two syllables of a root and some suffixes) plus predictable word stress. Stress is fixed by word size and tone, not weight: disyllables are stressed on the first syllable whatever their tone or vowel length; words of three or more syllables are stressed on the second syllable when toneless (or when H sits on the second syllable), but on the first syllable when H is lexically on the first syllable. Stress therefore stays in a left-edge two-syllable window. Earlier in the same section: 'a high pitch is also a correlate of stress in toneless words, but stress and high pitch could not coincide when lexical H is present'; where stress and H are on different syllables, stress is still marked by vowel quality (unstressed vowels centralize) and intensity, and speakers identify it on the first syllable. Adding syllables to a disyllable (6a-c) moves stress from sigma-1 to sigma-2 unless H is on sigma-1.
new_statements.exceptions: None beyond the tonal conditioning itself; the only stated deviation from the default (sigma-2 in longer words) is an initial lexical H, which pulls stress to sigma-1. Weight is explicitly excluded for disyllables ('regardless of lexical tone or vowel duration'), and the examples /iːbɨxi/ [iːˈbɨxi], /taːtasai/ [taːˈtasəi] show a long first vowel not attracting stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Gil Burgoin 2021 (JIPA): data from two female speakers (thirties) of the Tupuri village variety, one of the localities of the Baborigame nucleus, Guadalupe y Calvo, Chihuahua; the paper notes a possible three-way dialect split Baborigame (center) / Nabogame (south) / Venadito (north) after Molinari, Ruiz & Nolasco 1995. Bascom 1982: 'The Baborigame dialect is the larger of two major dialects; the other is spoken in and around Nabogame' (p. 271); the sketch is based on Baborigame speakers. Both works therefore describe the Baborigame variety.

new_statements.relation_note: Bascom 1982 says stress is non-contrastive and fluctuates freely in many words, i.e. no fixed placement, whereas the catalog's existing statements (Gil Burgoin 2021 AMP 9, and the JIPA Illustration read above) describe stress as fully predictable from word size plus weight/tone within a left-edge two-syllable window. Both agree the language has two tone levels (Bascom's H/L equipollent system vs Gil Burgoin's privative H or L). Gil Burgoin's first-hand acoustic data (1200-2000-word corpora, two speakers, Baborigame) explicitly supersede Bascom's line, which the existing statement already flags as superseded. Bascom's data are also Baborigame dialect.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two tones (p. 271, phoneme chart: 'Tone: there are two tones, high tone /´/ and low tone (unmarked)', scanned reads the acute as /*/) and vowel length interpreted as geminate clusters. Stress is stated to be non-contrastive and to fluctuate freely in many words; no placement rule, no domain, no interaction with tone is given. (The sentence reads 'It is freely fluctuation' sic in the original.) The Plural (pp. 307-312) and Stems/Number (pp. 347-352) sections were scanned as well and contain no further stress statement.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the sketch gives no rule to have exceptions from. It refers the compiler to Bascom's 1965 Proto-Tepiman dissertation 'for a more complete phonemic statement' (p. 273).

readall_conflicts: Two disagreements. (1) Bascom 1982 (in Langacker ed. 1982, p. 272) says 'Stress is noncontrastive. It is freely fluctuation in many words' and gives no placement, whereas Gil Burgoin's two 2021 papers (AMP 9 in the existing statements; the JIPA Illustration read here) describe stress as fully predictable, confined to the first two syllables (sigma-1 in disyllables; sigma-1 or sigma-2 in longer words; never final). Gil Burgoin's first-hand acoustic work supersedes Bascom's impressionistic line. (2) Within Gil Burgoin's own work the placement facts agree but the conditioning mechanism differs: AMP 9 (privative L analysis) says longer words stress the first heavy syllable in the window (long vowel or coda) else sigma-2, with an L-toned long initial vowel repelling stress; the JIPA Illustration (privative H analysis) says stress is predictable 'from the size and the tonal pattern of the word', with no role for weight: toneless 3+-syllable words take sigma-2 even with a long first vowel (/iːbɨxi/ [iːˈbɨxi], /taːtasai/ [taːˈtasəi]) and an initial lexical H pulls stress to sigma-1. The catalog's 'weight-sensitive within a two-syllable window' wording should be qualified: the same author's IPA Illustration treats the sigma-1/sigma-2 alternation as tone-driven, not weight-driven.
